People are disappointed because learning the "pendulum arbitration" story is an important part of growing up.

The initial idea is that Mr A arbitrates disputes between Mr R and Mr D. But Mr D has noticed that Mr A tends to split the difference. So Mr D tries to take advantage by exaggerating his side of the dispute. Eventually Mr R realises how this works and exaggerates his claim, in the opposite direction. Having the Arbiter split-the-difference has lead to polarization.

The follow up idea is pendulum arbitration. Each side states the remedy that they seek and the Arbiter is restricted to picking one or the other. He swings side to side and doesn't rest in the middle.

I don't think pendulum arbitration is such a good idea. If Mr R is 100% in the right, he will want Justice, while Mr D will regard compromise as a win (because it departs from Justice in his direction). The arbitrator ends up choosing between a hardline judgement and a compromise judgement. The temptation to split the difference and go for a compromise still ends up making mischief.

But to return to Jordan Peterson: hoping to unite people by splitting the difference is an idea for the under twenty fives. Older people know the pendulum arbitration story, perhaps because they have lived it. Older people know the danger and don't fall into the trap. Seeing the crusty, old psychology professor give us naive-young-man wisdom is disconcerting.
